scenes.tts: Fasting blood holds insulin at a few tens of picomolar. That is about one insulin molecule for every trillion molecules of water. Every pathway in this course rests on measuring something that scarce. How can anyone do it? Rozz-uh-lynn Yalow and Solomon Berson found a way, and it began as an unexpected by-product of a different experiment.
scenes.visual: A crowd of grey dots fills the frame with one yellow insulin dot hidden in it; a question mark. Then the two names appear.

Every pathway in this course rests on measuring something that scarce. How can anyone do it? Rosalyn Yalow and Solomon Berson found a way, and it began as an unexpected by-product of a different experiment.

scenes.tts: They were testing whether people with adult-onset diabetes destroy insulin too fast. So they tagged insulin with radioactive iodine, injected it, and followed the radioactivity as it left the blood. In people already treated with insulin, it left more slowly, because something in their blood was holding it. They argued that this something was an antibody. Immunologists of the day doubted that a protein as small as insulin could raise antibodies. Then they used it as a scale.
scenes.visual: Two blood lanes. Tagged insulin dots flow through the top lane but catch on cups in the bottom lane; the cups are labelled antibody and carried into the next scene.

In people already treated with insulin, it left more slowly, because something in their blood was holding it. They argued that this something was an antibody. scenes.tts: Take a tube. Put in a fixed, small amount of antibody. Add a fixed, small amount of radioactive insulin. Every tube gets the same amounts. The label is radioactive, so a counter can find it. The antibody has only a few binding sites, and the labelled insulin fills them.
scenes.visual: A tube grows around the antibody bar; labelled insulin drops in and seats in every cup; a gauge of label held by the antibody fills.
scenes.narration: Take a tube. Put in a fixed, small amount of antibody. Add a fixed, small amount of radioactive insulin. Every tube gets the same amounts. The label is radioactive, so a counter can find it. The antibody has only a few binding sites, and the labelled insulin fills them.

scenes.tts: Now add the blood sample. Its own insulin carries no label, so it competes with the labelled insulin for the same few sites. A little sample insulin displaces a few labelled molecules, and a lot displaces many. The more insulin the patient had, the less radioactivity ends up on the antibody.
scenes.visual: Unlabelled sample insulin enters and pushes labelled insulin out of the cups; the gauge falls, a little then a lot, with a reset between.
scenes.narration: Now add the blood sample. Its own insulin carries no label, so it competes with the labelled insulin for the same few sites. A little sample insulin displaces a few labelled molecules, and a lot displaces many. The more insulin the patient had, the less radioactivity ends up on the antibody.

scenes.tts: Now repeat the test with known amounts of insulin. Each tube holds the same antibody and the same labelled insulin. Those results build a curve. Separate the bound label from the free label, count each, and read the patient's concentration from the curve. This is the radioimmunoassay. It works from nanomolar down to a fraction of a picomolar.
scenes.visual: A plot is built point by point: more insulin, less label bound. The patient's count is read across to the curve and down to a concentration.

scenes.tts: An antibody can tell cortisol from corticosterone, two steroids that differ by one hydroxyl group. So the assay is only as selective as its antibody. Bioassays measured what a hormone does. This one counts how much is there. Keep this rule: more hormone in the sample means less label on the antibody.
scenes.visual: Two similar chips either side of an antibody cup; then what a bioassay measures against what this counts; then the rule as an arrow.
